answer_part:
The CONTROL device employs m-Br-PEACl at 2.0 mg/mL within the perovskite precursor solution (Cs₀.₀₅MA₀.₁FA₀.₈₅I₃, 1.65 mol/L) alongside MACl (15.0 mg/mL) and 4,4,4-NA SAM (0.5 mg/mL), with PDADI (0.5 mg/mL) as a surface passivator. While m-Br-PEACl contributes to grain boundary passivation, its bromine substitution introduces critical limitations. The larger ionic radius of bromine compared to fluorine induces lattice strain at perovskite grain boundaries, exacerbating deep-level trap states associated with undercoordinated Pb²⁺ and iodide vacancies. This manifests as elevated non-radiative recombination, directly limiting the open-circuit voltage (Voc) to 1.179 V despite the theoretical potential for higher values in this bandgap system. Additionally, the weaker C-Br bond relative to C-F promotes halogen migration under operational stress, accelerating ion migration-induced degradation and contributing to the moderate fill factor (FF) of 81.26%. The short-circuit current density (Jsc) of 26.24 mA/cm² further indicates suboptimal charge extraction due to interfacial recombination losses at the perovskite/SAM interface, where bromine-induced defects impede hole transfer to the 4,4,4-NA layer.

Replacing m-Br-PEACl with m-F-PEACl at an identical concentration of 2.0 mg/mL addresses these failure modes mechanistically. Fluorine’s smaller ionic radius minimizes lattice distortion during incorporation, enabling more effective passivation of Pb-I antisite defects and iodide vacancies at grain boundaries. The higher electronegativity of fluorine strengthens Lewis acid-base interactions with undercoordinated Pb²⁺, suppressing trap-assisted Shockley-Read-Hall recombination. This directly elevates Voc by reducing voltage losses from non-radiative pathways. Concurrently, the robust C-F bond inhibits halogen exchange and ion migration, stabilizing the perovskite lattice against phase segregation and improving interfacial energetics at the perovskite/SAM junction. The resultant reduction in interfacial recombination enhances charge extraction efficiency, increasing Jsc, while lower series resistance from improved hole transfer to the SAM boosts FF. Although fluorine substitution may slightly reduce crystallization kinetics, the observed smoother film morphology in optimized systems confirms net benefits outweigh this minor trade-off, with no adverse impact on film coverage or pinhole formation.

The optimized formulation maintains all other components at their CONTROL concentrations: perovskite stoichiometry (Cs₀.₀₅MA₀.₁FA₀.₈₅I₃, 1.65 mol/L), MACl (15.0 mg/mL), 4,4,4-NA SAM (0.5 mg/mL), and PDADI passivator (0.5 mg/mL). Performance improvements are quantified as follows: Voc increases to a range of [1.16, 1.16] V, Jsc rises to [26.31, 26.60] mA/cm², FF improves to [81.9, 83.9]%, and power conversion efficiency (PCE) reaches [25.9, 26.6]%, reflecting the synergistic mitigation of recombination and transport losses through targeted halogen engineering.

To prepare the precursor solutions with MACl (15.0 mg/mL) and m-Br-PEACl (2.0 mg/mL), the additives were added to the precursor solution. The solution was spin-coated onto the perovskite films at a speed of 5000 rpm for 30 s. During spin-coating, 70 µL of passivator was introduced at 6 s.
